# Benji Wise

> Benji Wise is a builder in Boston who directs AI models to write software and holds the taste himself — a practice he calls vibe-coding. He is a senior at Northeastern University studying business administration with a finance concentration and an environmental studies minor, and is open to work in 2026. His site, benjiwise.com, is published under the name The BenAri.

His stated position: "Optimization is the easy half. People are the hard half. I work in the gap between the two."

Recent output, as stated on the site: ten systems vibe-coded in about eight weeks, 288 commits, three of them running 24/7 in production. His summary of the method: "AI writes the code; I hold the taste." The recurring techniques are multi-agent orchestration, pgvector RAG, MCP tool servers, and live-broker trading.

How he works, in his own framing: he starts with a conversation, not a spec — sitting with the people who will actually use the thing to find the problem they really have, usually not the one written on the ticket. Then he builds the smallest version that solves it and gets it into their hands early, learning from real use instead of guessing. He would rather ship one feature people reach for every day than ten they have to be talked into. He does not write the code line by line; he directs the models and spends his own attention on what is worth building at all.

There is a short list of things he says he won't do: build for problems nobody has; oversell, because saying plainly what a tool can't do is what gets it adopted; or call something working before it's verified. His example of the last point: he built an AI trading strategy, ran the research, found no real edge, and rebuilt it from scratch — "I'd rather retire my own work than defend it."

Based in Boston. Available in 2026.

## Pages

- [Benji Wise — portfolio](https://benjiwise.com/): The landing page. Covers who he is, three selected projects, and the approach quoted above. The projects are framed as "01 — Built to be used" (benji-ai, the assistant), "02 — Tested to break" (the trading system, titled on the page as "(NOT SO) INTELLIGENCE-OFFICE"), and "03 — Worth watching" (a sales race board).
- [Benari — a system that can read itself](https://benjiwise.com/benari.html): A personal assistant Benji Wise texts on WhatsApp, vibe-coded end to end, with an instrumentation layer he says has found more than testing did. Thirty-four tools cover calendar, email, tasks and notes; anything that sends or deletes stops and waits for a typed yes — a gate in the code rather than an instruction in the prompt, so the model cannot talk its way past it. Seventy-one named events make every turn traceable: what it recalled, what it called, how long each stage took, a layer that caught three problems before they reached him and that he says no test would have found. Four of its tools point at its own source, read-only and sandboxed, so it can open a file in its own repo, search the tree and read its commit log to explain its own behaviour. A turn re-sends its persona, rules and tool list up to six times as the model works; the prompt is split so every send after the first is served from cache. Background agents keep it current between conversations — one measures how often it gets a memory wrong and tunes its own threshold on the result. Voice is live end to end. A new domain is a row in a table, not a rewrite. Running since June; production is WhatsApp via Twilio. The chat thread shown on the page is scripted with invented names.
- [Signal Desk — it traded its own best worst ideas](https://benjiwise.com/signal-desk.html): An autonomous trading system that screens, decides, sizes and places its own orders through a live Robinhood account with no human in the loop. Its record, 9 June to 31 July 2026: 37 trading days, down 5.0% while the market rose 1.4%, 15 round trips in a single $1,500 personal account, from 233 recommendations and 32 filled orders. The loss is not the point. Because it logged what it skipped, it can be graded against itself, and its confidence ran backwards: the picks it chose to trade are down 24.7% while the ones it skipped are down 1.0%, and its high-conviction picks did worst of all at −31.3%. The cause was concentration — 25 companies, with two names it kept re-entering — and only trailing stops kept a bad quarter from being a wipeout. It also caught its own bookkeeping drifting from reality: its ledger claimed a $91.46 loss where the broker said $43.86, overstating the damage by more than the damage, so every published figure is broker-sourced rather than app-sourced. The code was frozen on 22 June, so everything after that date is one unchanged build running unattended, which is what makes the record worth reading. The equity curve replays every fill in FIFO order against daily closes, benchmarked to SPY over the identical window. Sample far too small to separate a bad strategy from bad luck. Not investment advice.

## Optional

- [Sales race track](https://benjiwise.com/race-board/index.html?demo=1): A retro leaderboard that turns a sales floor's targets into a race on the office TV. Every rep is a car, a pace line shows who is on track, and 100% sets off the checkered flag. Dependency-free, built to run all day on cheap TV hardware. The public demo runs on mock data with fictional names.
